Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent’s action. We introduce MemCredit , a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility . MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 % 86.57\% SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67 % 65.67\% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.

A memory that appears less related to the current observation may be critical for avoiding an incorrect action, whereas a highly relevant memory can be redundant.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that search, browse, invoke tools, and interact with online environments over extended trajectories ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Unlike single-turn generation, such interaction is inherently stateful : a correct decision may depend on an earlier user constraint, previously observed information, or a failed action that should not be repeated. As trajectories grow, retaining the full interaction history becomes increasingly inefficient, making memory management essential for long-horizon agents ( Park et al., 2023 ; Packer et al., 2023 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ) . Moreover, access to long context does not guarantee effective use of its contents, as performance can vary substantially with how relevant information is positioned and organized ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Existing memory systems address this challenge through recency-based retention, semantic retrieval, trajectory compression, structured memory banks, and learned memory policies ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Despite these differences, memory selection is still commonly driven by recency, semantic similarity, salience, or learned retrieval scores. Such signals identify information that is related to the current state, but relatedness does not necessarily imply value for sequential decision making.

As illustrated in Figure 1 , a recently observed item may be highly similar to the current observation yet contribute little to the next action. Conversely, an earlier constraint, failed attempt, or less similar piece of evidence may be critical for avoiding an incorrect decision. This reveals a fundamental mismatch between information retrieval and agent memory management: semantic relevance measures whether a memory matches the current state, whereas decision utility measures whether it improves the agent’s decision . We therefore ask: would the agent make a worse decision if a particular memory were unavailable? This formulation treats memory value as state-, reference-context-, and policy-dependent, and casts memory management as a fine-grained credit-assignment problem rather than relevance ranking. It is related to recent experience- and skill-based agents that evaluate reusable knowledge through downstream outcomes ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Tu et al., 2026 ) , but operates at the granularity of individual memories. Controlled intervention experiments support this distinction (Sec. 4.3 ; Table 3 and Figure 5 ). Across 1,041 context-conditional interventions from 45 ALFWorld tasks, 86.9 % 86.9\% produce no measurable behavioral change, indicating that memory utility is highly sparse. Average utility rises to 0.176 0.176 in failure contexts but is only 0.029 0.029 outside failure states, while semantic relevance has almost no overall correlation with counterfactual utility ( ρ = − 0.011 \rho=-0.011 ). These results suggest that semantic similarity is an unreliable proxy for whether a memory is consequential to the current decision.

Motivated by these findings, we introduce MemCredit , a framework for decision-time memory arbitration in long-horizon agents. MemCredit decomposes interaction histories into atomic memories and uses controlled counterfactual interventions to estimate their marginal decision contributions. The resulting credits supervise a lightweight utility estimator, amortizing the cost of counterfactual evaluation. At inference time, MemCredit separates candidate recall from memory arbitration : semantic relevance retrieves a broad candidate pool, while predicted utility determines which memories are retained under a fixed token budget. The underlying agent policy remains unchanged and requires no additional environment interaction at deployment. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) and WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) . On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 % 86.57\% SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, outperforming BM25 retrieval by 20.90 20.90 percentage points. With a 750-token budget, it reaches 90.30 % 90.30\% SR@50, compared with 81.34 % 81.34\% for BM25, showing larger gains under tighter context constraints. On WebShop, MemCredit achieves the highest task score of 0.612 0.612 while using only 152.1 152.1 memory tokens per decision. Compared with MemArbiter, the strongest non-MemCredit baseline, it improves the score from 0.586 0.586 to 0.612 0.612 while using about 2.8 × 2.8\times fewer memory tokens; relative to BM25, memory usage is reduced by approximately 3.9 × 3.9\times . As shown in Figure 2 , MemCredit yields a clear performance–memory Pareto improvement and also reduces repeated searches, invalid actions, and trajectory length. Our contributions are threefold:

• We formulate decision-time memory credit assignment , distinguishing semantic relevance from the state- and policy-conditional marginal contribution of an individual memory, and show that such utility is sparse, state dependent, and poorly captured by relevance. • We propose MemCredit , which estimates fine-grained memory credit through controlled counterfactual intervention and distills it into an amortized utility estimator for budget-aware memory arbitration. • We demonstrate on ALFWorld and WebShop that separating relevance-based candidate recall from utility-based arbitration improves both task performance and context efficiency, especially under tight historical-memory budgets. Interaction histories are organized into atomic memories, whose policy-conditional decision utility is estimated through controlled counterfactual interventions and distilled into a lightweight utility estimator. Agent memory supports long-horizon interaction through experience retrieval ( Park et al., 2023 ) , long-term storage ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) , tiered context management ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , and evolving memory structures ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . Recent methods further compress trajectories into structured states ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , learn bounded memory updates ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , or select compressed blocks using the query and working memory ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . MemArbiter ( Dong et al., 2026 ) addresses the Memory–Action Gap : retrievable information may still fail to guide actions. It organizes history into functional banks and controls memory presentation through demand, relevance, and temporal signals. Its arbitration uses predefined signals rather than intervention-derived memory credits. Closer approaches explicitly evaluate memory utility. CMI ( Srivastava, 2026 ) scores memories through controlled interventions in conversational tasks. CICL ( Guan et al., 2026 ) estimates decision-oriented utility and assembles selected evidence into budgeted memory cards. MeClear ( Yang et al., 2026 ) combines leave-one-out screening with sampled Shapley attribution to capture interactions and suppress harmful memories. MemCredit focuses on state-conditioned, item-level credit assignment for sequential decisions. It collects credits through paired replay from matched environment states under a fixed action policy, then trains a lightweight estimator for token-budgeted selection without additional runtime environment interaction. Single-removal attribution can mask redundancy among interacting memories; Sec. 3.4 discusses how conditional reference contexts mitigate this.

Effective memory use requires historical experience to improve downstream behavior. Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) stores feedback-derived reflections in episodic memory, ExpeL ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) extracts transferable insights from agent trajectories, and SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026 ) distills trajectories into reusable skills. More explicitly, D2Skill ( Tu et al., 2026 ) evaluates skills through paired rollouts under the same policy, while memory-augmented RL optimizes memory updates using trajectory-level rewards ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . These approaches connect experience reuse with behavioral improvement, but their credit signals mainly target reusable skills or memory-update trajectories rather than individual memories at a specific decision state. MemCredit instead performs decision-time credit assignment for individual memory items. For memory m i m_{i} at state s t s_{t} , it estimates marginal decision utility by comparing decision quality with and without that memory under the same policy, environment state, and reference context. The resulting counterfactual credits supervise a lightweight utility estimator for budget-aware arbitration, while leaving the agent policy unchanged. Semantic relevance is used for candidate recall, whereas predicted utility determines final memory priority.

We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop . For ALFWorld, following the evaluation protocol of MemArbiter ( Dong et al., 2026 ) , we use all 134 tasks from the out-of-distribution evaluation split, with a maximum of 50 interaction steps per episode. Its deterministic dynamics allow factual and counterfactual decisions to be replayed from the same reconstructed environment state. WebShop evaluates long-horizon Web interaction, where agents must preserve user constraints, product attributes, and previous search outcomes. We use a 50-task development set and report final evaluation on 200 tasks over a 10K-product catalog.

All main experiments use Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 with deterministic decoding. The primary Qwen policy is served with vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) . At each step, every method receives the same task goal, current observation, previous interaction outcome, and method-specific memory context. The current observation is excluded from the memory budget, which constrains historical information only. For ALFWorld, admissible actions are provided to all methods, and we evaluate historical-memory budgets of 500 and 750 tokens. The agent policy, action parser, environment interface, and interaction limits are kept fixed across methods. For cross-model evaluation, we replace only the action-generation model with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct , DeepSeek-V3 , or GPT-5.4 , while retaining the same memory construction, state parsing, prompts, and 500-token memory budget. Additional implementation and prompting details are provided in the Appendix.

We compare MemCredit with Flat Recency ( Dong et al., 2026 ) , which retains recent history; BM25 Retrieval ( Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009 ) , which ranks memories by lexical relevance; Dense Retrieval ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) , which uses semantic similarity; Failure-Aware Retrieval , a heuristic that prioritizes recent failure-related memories, inspired by failure-aware experience reuse ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2026 ) ; and State-Aware Retrieval , a heuristic that selects memories aligned with the current interaction state ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . We also evaluate MemArbiter ( Dong et al., 2026 ) , which controls memory presentation through functional banks, dynamic signals, and a temporal gate. Utility-only and relevance–utility hybrid variants of MemCredit are evaluated in the ablation study.

For ALFWorld, we collect 1,041 valid context-conditional interventions from 45 tasks , following the protocol of the Methodology section: reference contexts are sampled at occupancy levels α ∈ { 0 , 1 4 , 1 2 , 3 4 , 1 } \alpha\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{4},1\} under the 500-token budget, and both branches are replayed from the same reconstructed environment state with a fixed continuation protocol; every retained sample passes the reconstruction check. Supervision comes from task-disjoint training and development splits, and test-task outcomes are excluded from estimator fitting and threshold selection, as required by the collection protocol. For WebShop, we apply the same protocol to a disjoint training set of trajectories. The resulting memory–state–utility triples train the utility estimator, which is frozen before evaluation on the 200-task test set. Further details are provided in the Appendix.

For ALFWorld, we report SR@50 overall and by task category, together with post-failure recovery and failed-action repetition. For WebShop, we report task performance, redundant interactions, and average memory usage. Counterfactual analysis measures utility sparsity, state dependence, and relevance–utility correlation. Utility prediction is evaluated with task-disjoint 5-fold GroupKFold using Spearman correlation, AUPRC, and AUROC. Table 1 compares memory-management strategies under the same Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 policy on 134 unseen ALFWorld tasks. Under the tighter 500-token budget, MemCredit achieves 86.57% SR@50, outperforming BM25, State-Aware Retrieval, and MemArbiter. This corresponds to a 20.90 20.90 -point gain over BM25. The improvement spans all six task categories and is particularly pronounced on Heat , Cool , and Pick Two , where MemCredit improves over BM25 by 30.43 30.43 , 28.57 28.57 , and 35.30 35.30 points, respectively, indicating the benefit of utility-aware arbitration for tasks with stronger historical dependencies. The advantage persists as the memory budget increases. At 750 tokens, MemCredit reaches 90.30% SR@50, compared with 81.34 % 81.34\% for BM25, 85.07 % 85.07\% for State-Aware Retrieval, and 85.82 % 85.82\% for MemArbiter. The margin over BM25 decreases from 20.90 20.90 points at 500 tokens to 8.96 8.96 points at 750 tokens, suggesting that explicit memory arbitration is particularly valuable under tighter context constraints. Behavioral metrics show the same pattern: at 500 tokens, MemCredit achieves the highest recovery rate and the lowest failed-action repetition rate. Overall, these results show that MemCredit improves both task success and post-failure behavior through decision-aware memory selection.

Table 2 evaluates task performance and interaction efficiency on 200 WebShop tasks over a 10K-product catalog. MemCredit achieves the highest task score of 0.612 , outperforming BM25, Dense Retrieval, State-Aware Retrieval, and the strongest structured-memory baseline, MemArbiter. At the same time, MemCredit uses only 152.1 historical memory tokens per decision, compared with 427.6 427.6 for MemArbiter and 597.0 597.0 for BM25, corresponding to reductions of 64.4% and 74.5% , respectively. MemCredit also yields more efficient interaction behavior. Compared with MemArbiter, repeated searches decrease from 0.227 0.227 to 0.213 0.213 , invalid actions from 0.324 0.324 to 0.316 0.316 , and average trajectory length from 12.3 12.3 to 12.0 12.0 steps. Similar improvements are observed over relevance-based retrieval methods. As visualized in Figure 2 , MemCredit therefore shifts the agent toward a more favorable performance–memory frontier, improving task quality while substantially reducing the historical context required at each decision step. We further examine whether MemCredit depends on the underlying action-generation model. We replace only the action model while keeping memory construction, state parsing, prompts, interaction limits, and the 500-token memory budget fixed. As shown in Figure 4 , MemCredit outperforms Flat Recency, BM25, and MemArbiter in almost all model and step-limit settings across Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct , Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 , DeepSeek-V3 , and GPT-5.4 : the single exception is SR@50 under GPT-5.4, where BM25 scores marginally higher. Although absolute performance varies across backbones and interaction horizons, the advantage of utility-aware memory arbitration holds across nearly all settings, indicating that MemCredit is not tied to a specific LLM. chunks.section: Relevance is not a stable proxy for decision utility .
chunks.text: Across the combined intervention set, semantic relevance has essentially no overall association with marginal utility. Moreover, the relationship changes with task coverage: the dense subset yields ρ = − 0.191 \rho=-0.191 , whereas the broader 44-task subset yields ρ = + 0.135 \rho=+0.135 . Thus, semantic similarity is not a stable estimate of a memory’s marginal decision value.

chunks.text: Mean credit is 0.054 0.054 , yet 86.9 % 86.9\% of interventions produce no measurable change. Most memories therefore have little effect at a given step, while a small subset accounts for most of the observed impact.

Failure-context interventions have a mean utility of 0.176 0.176 , compared with 0.029 0.029 outside failure states. As shown in Figure 5 (b–c), failure contexts exhibit the strongest effects, while several other state categories are substantially weaker. chunks.section: Utility is predictable beyond relevance and failure cues .
chunks.text: Relevance-only features provide little predictive signal ( ρ = − 0.031 \rho=-0.031 , AUPRC 0.097 0.097 , AUROC 0.483 0.483 ), while failure-related features are more informative (AUPRC 0.184 0.184 , AUROC 0.658 0.658 ). chunks.section: Decision utility is the main source of improvement .
chunks.text: Replacing utility-based ranking with BM25 reduces SR@50 from 84.33 % 84.33\% to 65.67 % 65.67\% . A failure-only heuristic reaches 70.15 % 70.15\% , indicating that simply prioritizing failure-related memories does not explain the improvement. These results highlight the importance of estimating the decision value of individual memories.

chunks.section: Relevance is more useful for recall than arbitration .
chunks.text: Directly combining relevance and predicted utility ( λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 ) achieves 78.36 % 78.36\% , 5.97 5.97 points below utility-only ranking. This supports our design choice of using relevance for candidate recall while relying on predicted utility for final memory arbitration.

chunks.section: The gain is not a failure shortcut .
chunks.text: Removing explicit failure/state indicators further improves SR@50 from 84.33 % 84.33\% to 86.57 % 86.57\% , which is used as the primary MemCredit configuration. Together with the weaker Failure-Aware baseline, this suggests that MemCredit captures broader state–memory interactions rather than relying on explicit failure cues. Overall, the ablation identifies utility-aware arbitration—the context-conditional credit-per-token selection of Sec. 3.4 —as the main source of improvement, while direct relevance interpolation and failure-specific heuristics provide weaker alternatives. Additional budget analyses are reported in the Appendix.

We introduced MemCredit, a decision-utility-based memory framework for long-horizon agents. Rather than treating semantic relevance as the primary criterion for memory selection, MemCredit estimates the context-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through counterfactual credit assignment, while keeping the action policy frozen and avoiding additional environment interaction at deployment. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that this principle improves memory arbitration under limited context budgets. Our analysis further reveals that decision utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and only weakly captured by semantic relevance. These findings suggest that future agent memory systems should optimize not only what information is retrieved, but which memories are most consequential for the decisions that follow.

Hardware and inference. All same-model ALFWorld evaluations use Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 served with vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) on A800-80GB GPUs, with a 4096-token context window, temperature 0, and seed 42. All compared methods use the same action protocol, parser, environment, and admissible-command hints. The current observation is included in the base prompt and excluded from the historical-memory budget. Pipeline validation. The sharded evaluation pipeline was validated by rerunning BM25@500, which reproduces the frozen result ( 65.67 % 65.67\% SR@50) up to the execution-order variance documented below: across repeated executions, task-level outcomes agree on at least 94 % 94\% of the 134 tasks, and single-run aggregate SR varies by up to ± 3 \pm 3 pp. The agent uses no Python-side randomness; the residual flips trace to GPU-side logit nondeterminism on near-ties under temperature-0 decoding. Memory budgets of 500 and 750 tokens apply only to historical memory.

Utility label generation. Intervention labels follow Eq. 9 : the observed one-step credit is the difference between the two branches’ environment rewards, r + i − r − i r^{+i}-r^{-i} , where each branch is executed by the same frozen policy from the same reconstructed state and differs only in the rendered inclusion of the target memory. For ALFWorld, the step reward r r is instantiated with an environment-grounded outcome score taking values in { + 1 , 0 , − 1 } \{+1,0,-1\} : + 1 +1 if the episode is won at this step; − 1 -1 if the chosen action is not in the admissible set or repeats a previously failed action; and 0 0 for a valid but neutral action. Reference contexts are sampled at occupancy levels α ∈ { 0 , 1 4 , 1 2 , 3 4 , 1 } \alpha\in\{0,\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{4},1\} under the budget, so the factual branch A A and its reference S = A ∖ { m i } S=A\setminus\{m_{i}\} cover isolated, partial, and near-budget contexts. Each pair is executed once (no repeated sampling), and samples whose reconstructed state differs from the recorded one are discarded by the reconstruction check; all 1,041 retained samples pass it. Primary causal analyses use the single-removal reference context S = C t ∖ { m i } S=C_{t}\setminus\{m_{i}\} for the main statistics.

WebShop catalog audit. The 10K-product catalog is a uniform subsample of the standard WebShop catalog. For all 200 evaluated instructions, the target product and its required options are present in the catalog, and the target is retrievable within the top-10 search results under the BM25 index used by the environment (Recall@10/20/50 = 100%), so the evaluation is not confounded by missing catalog entries. The reward semantics are identical to standard WebShop; because the catalog is a 10K subset of the full catalog, scores are not directly comparable to full-catalog literature values.

Primary uncertainty estimates use task-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. We report dense-only and broad-only statistics separately to assess sensitivity to task coverage. Evaluation protocol. Utility predictors are evaluated using 5-fold GroupKFold split by task ID, preventing intervention samples from the same task from appearing in both training and evaluation folds; main results are reported in Table 4 . Features. Relevance-only features contain semantic relevance and recency age; failure-only features contain previous-action failure, failure-related indicators, and state-type features; content features contain inference-time memory and state descriptors. The full estimator adds the context descriptors x ctx x_{\mathrm{ctx}} (token-level overlap with the selected context, candidate-entity coverage, per-type context counts, and budget occupancy), which expose whether a candidate contributes information already represented in the selected context. A context-blind control omits these descriptors. No counterfactual outcome or intervention-result fields are available to the predictor. Estimator. The primary ExtraTrees ( Geurts et al., 2006 ) model uses 300 trees, maximum depth 8, and minimum leaf size 8. Ridge regression with α = 1 \alpha=1 is used as a simpler control. NDCG diagnostic. NDCG@5 is omitted from the main text because 86.9 % 86.9\% of utility labels are exactly zero, producing extensive ranking ties. The shuffled-label control obtains NDCG@5 0.301 0.301 , compared with 0.131 0.131 for the full estimator, indicating that this metric is not informative under the current label distribution. We therefore rely primarily on Spearman correlation, AUPRC, and AUROC.

The hybrid ablation variant uses a fixed interpolation coefficient λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 , selected before final evaluation. The Failure-Aware baseline adds a fixed bonus to failure-related memories while preserving the same retrieval and memory budget. No post-hoc tuning is performed on the final 134-task evaluation set. A larger 750-token budget raises utility-only ALFWorld SR from 84.33 % 84.33\% to 88.81 % 88.81\% , and the primary MemCredit configuration from 86.57 % 86.57\% to 90.30 % 90.30\% . Additional failure-density analyses stratify tasks using bins fixed from baseline trajectories before comparing methods.

We further examine whether the benefit of MemCredit is restricted to failure-intensive trajectories. Using the frozen BM25 trajectories, we compute the failure density of each ALFWorld task and partition the 134 tasks into low-, medium-, and high-failure-density terciles. The resulting partition is fixed and applied to both BM25 and MemCredit, avoiding method-dependent grouping. As shown in Figure 6 , MemCredit consistently outperforms BM25 across all three groups. The SR@50 improvements are + 20.0 +20.0 , + 15.9 +15.9 , and + 20.0 +20.0 percentage points for the low-, medium-, and high-failure groups, respectively. The paired task-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals remain above zero in all three terciles: [ + 6.7 , + 33.3 ] [+6.7,+33.3] , [ + 4.5 , + 29.5 ] [+4.5,+29.5] , and [ + 8.9 , + 33.3 ] [+8.9,+33.3] . This result complements the intervention analysis in Sec. 4.3 . Although individual memories exhibit substantially larger marginal utility in failure contexts, the end-to-end advantage of utility-aware arbitration is not confined to failure-heavy tasks. Failure context therefore represents an important source of memory utility, but not the only setting in which decision-aware memory selection is useful. Figure 6.
